This work marks a significant step in understanding transfer learning for GNNs and highlights its practical applications in real-world scenarios. In Europe, buses transport approximately 25% of all public passengers, 
with a significant portion using ticket machines to pay their fares. 
This research focuses on the most common methods used to obtain tickets 
from these machines, which are then employed in a variety of attacks. 
One such attack, known as the "fare-evasion" attack, aims to avoid paying 
the fare by exploiting the most popular ticketing methods. 
Another form of attack, the "fare-beating" attack, aims to cheat the system 
by using a combination of ticket types to pay less than the full fare. 
Both types of attacks are analyzed in this research, with the fare-evasion 
attack yielding a success rate of 100% and the fare-beating attack yielding 
a success rate of 71.4%. 
A potential countermeasure to prevent fare-beating attacks is also presented. 
This research is the first to investigate fare evasion and fare beating on 
public transportation systems.

abuse of public transportation ticket machines and to encourage the development 
of more secure systems.

Additionally, this approach is validated through experiments using a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle navigating around obstacles to avoid collisions with a ground robot. We conducted an investigation into the polarization properties of 94 radio sources from the 87GB catalog with angular sizes spanning 2 inches to 36 inches, using the 37-meter Green Bank Telescope equipped with the Polarization Receiver Experiment. These results suggest a complex relationship between radio source morphology and polarization properties. This research introduces a class of stochastic advection problems to model turbulent transport, incorporating the key characteristics of turbulence - non-linearity, non-locality, and randomness - into a single equation. Utilizing techniques from hydrodynamic stability theory, we establish conditions for existence and uniqueness of solutions, as well as providing an estimate for their lifespan. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply our method to simulate the behavior of two-dimensional turbulent flows in channels and pipes, recovering the established statistical properties of these systems. Furthermore, we extend this framework to model turbulent transport in three-dimensional channels, verifying that it yields a solution that matches the established statistical properties of three-dimensional turbulent flows. Finally, we conduct a numerical analysis of the stochastic advection problem in a three-dimensional pipe to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach for solving turbulent transport problems in practice. This research provides a versatile mathematical framework for modeling turbulent transport, offering a valuable tool for simulating turbulent flows in various environments. It has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of simulations by capturing the key characteristics of turbulence and providing a reliable solution for practical applications. Graph Neural Networks have achieved significant success in various applications, but they are often hindered by the scarcity of labels, which can be mitigated by semi-supervised learning. A common approach to this problem involves refining node representations using a classifier, but this method has limitations as it fails to account for label information. In this research, we present an innovative framework that leverages a classifier to generate informative pseudo-labels, which are then incorporated into the node representations through an attention-based mechanism. Our approach outperforms existing methods in semi-supervised node classification and label propagation, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in multiple scenarios involving various label distributions and node types. Notably, our method excels in label propagation by achieving a 10.7% absolute improvement over state-of-the-art methods. Our source code is available for public access.

In plasma wakefield acceleration experiments, particularly in accelerator-based facilities like the AWAKE project, accurately understanding electron beam dynamics is crucial for optimal particle accelerator performance. We introduce an innovative, communication-efficient stochastic gradient descent (SGD) technique known as Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD). CA-SGD employs a data compression-decompression strategy to minimize communication during training of large, deep neural models. By strategically compressing model parameters and gradients at the client and decompressing them at the server, CA-SGD optimizes communication efficiency. Our analysis demonstrates that CA-SGD achieves a data compression ratio of 2:1 in a single round, and 4:1 in an N-Round AllReduce setting. Experimental results on ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100 datasets show that CA-SGD yields comparable convergence rates with significantly reduced communication requirements, up to 85% less for ImageNet-1K and 95% less for CIFAR-100. Moreover, our technique outperforms existing methods by enabling training of models on 128 GPUs with only 10 Gbps bandwidth, surpassing the current state-of-the-art of 40 Gbps required for training on 128 GPUs. In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access has the potential to significantly reduce latency and energy consumption, particularly when compared to traditional time division multiple access methods. This is because devices can immediately transmit data without needing to wait for scheduling information. However, the unstructured nature of grant-free access leads to significant interference and reduced overall performance. To mitigate this issue, a new approach is proposed in this paper, which involves designing specific sequences for individual devices to use during initial access attempts. By using these sequences, separate channels can be identified and isolated from one another, reducing interference and increasing overall performance. A novel optimization problem is formulated to determine the optimal sequence length and structure, and a solution is proposed through the use of iterative algorithms. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods, with performance gains of up to 10 dB and 5 dB observed in terms of area coverage and throughput, respectively. Furthermore, the method's scalability is evaluated and found to be effective even in scenarios with large numbers of devices. Overall, the approach is shown to be efficient and effective, with potential applications extending beyond massive machine-type communications to other areas such as IoT and ultra-wideband systems. The method's simplicity and effectiveness make it a promising solution for a wide range of communication systems. By adapting the axiomatic approach of Kontsevich, we develop an enumerative theory for such sheaves, which can be viewed as a specialized case of the axiomatic theory of moduli spaces proposed by Manin and Kontsevich. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the enumerative invariants of pure one-dimensional sheaves and those of curve counting in Calabi-Yau 3-folds, as described by Buchdahl and Gompf. This relationship is rooted in a geometric interpretation inspired by the work of Borcea and Alzati. In addition, we derive explicit formulas for the enumerative invariants in question. Specifically, we calculate the higher genus analogues of the Witten diagonal invariants for rank r and degree d sheaves, which generalizes earlier work by Buchdahl and Gompf for rank one. Moreover, we show that these formulas can be expressed through the use of hypergeometric functions, a connection that was first explored by Buchdahl in the context of rank one sheaves. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of enumerative invariants across various areas of mathematical physics and algebraic geometry. Specifically, we observe that the enumerative invariants we derive for rank one sheaves coincide with those obtained by Buchdahl, while they differ from those obtained by Gompf. This disparity highlights the distinct nature of enumerative invariants for pure one-dimensional sheaves, which cannot be reduced to the case of line bundles as initially suggested by Gompf. This work serves as a foundation for further research into the enumerative theory of pure one-dimensional sheaves, which we plan to explore in a forthcoming paper. In particular, we aim to establish a connection between the enumerative invariants of sheaves and those of Landau-Ginzburg theory, as described by Borcea and Alzati. Moreover, we will investigate the relationship between the enumerative invariants of sheaves and those of stable pairs, as proposed by Pandharipande and Siebert. We investigate the convergence of stochastic gradient descent with a constant step size for minimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions. Our analysis reveals that this method achieves an optimal $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate on a finite domain with $k$ iterations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this rate is inherent, even with an infinite search space, assuming that the function's level set has a finite diameter. Our findings also extend to non-smooth functions with H\"older continuous gradients, yielding a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/(\log k)^{\alpha-1/2})$. Additionally, we provide a precise error bound for stochastic gradient descent on non-smooth, strongly-convex functions with H\"older continuous gradients, showing that it converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/(\log k)^{\alpha})$. These results are verified through supporting numerical experiments. Our research is unique in that it provides a precise error bound for stochastic gradient descent on non-smooth functions and demonstrates that stochastic gradient descent with a constant step size can converge at the optimal rate for various classes of functions. Our findings also show that stochastic gradient descent can outperform its online first-order model counterpart in certain scenarios. Human vocal interactions can reveal insightful information about a person's 
cognitive behaviors, emotional states, and social connections. Entrainment, 
which involves synchronizing vocal characteristics with others, holds significant 
value in understanding human relationships. This study develops a novel method 
for measuring entrainment based on a specific type of synchronization called 
phase locking. This approach is applied to a diverse dataset of interactions 
from the Human Dynamics Project, yielding valuable insights into individuals' 
social patterns. Notably, our findings indicate that phase locking aligns with 
previous research on social connections, while also showing that it is more 
sensitive to detecting close relationships than other relevant metrics. Moreover, 
our analysis reveals that phase locking is more effective in identifying strong 
social bonds than other relevant metrics. This research contributes to a deeper 
understanding of entrainment and social dynamics by providing a more precise 
diagnosis of social connections based on phase locking and other relevant 
factors. Furthermore, our findings suggest that entrainment can be a valuable 
indicator of cognitive behaviors, emotional states, and social interactions. This 
knowledge can be applied to developing more accurate models for predicting 
cognitive behaviors, recognizing emotional states, and analyzing social 
interactions. Ultimately, our research aims to create more effective machine 
learning models for recognizing human behaviors. The code and data used in this 
study are available for public access at https://github.com/jean-pierre-le-cunff.

Glaciological problems, including those involving ice and gas interactions, can be represented by Stokes variational inequalities.  This paper presents a semi-discrete approximation of these inequalities in the form of a system of ordinary differential inequalities.  This system's well-posedness is established using a combination of the Banach fixed point theorem and energy methods.  It is shown that as spatial and temporal discretization parameters approach zero, the approximate system converges to the original inequalities.  This result is demonstrated under minimal assumptions.  Furthermore, under certain conditions, the approximate system can be seen as a time-stepping approximation of a variational inequality representing the equilibrium state of the glaciological problem.  This result is utilized to establish convergence rates for a time-discrete scheme when the problem's solution satisfies certain regularity conditions.  This paper's findings are illustrated through numerical experiments involving a two-dimensional ice sheet model.  Specifically, it examines the impact of various boundary conditions on the model's solution. To achieve this, we develop a novel unsupervised approach for pre-training deep networks using depth estimation, which leverages the inherent 3D structure of the environment to generate meaningful representations. Notably, we find that this pre-training approach can outperform traditional methods when applied to new domains, highlighting its potential for transfer learning. Our findings also reveal that the representations learned through depth estimation tend to capture spatial and structural information, whereas those learned through traditional unsupervised methods tend to capture more diverse and dynamic information. This work establishes inequalities that connect the entropy of a continuous random variable and its rank-order according to the probability density function, utilizing Kendall's tau as the order statistic. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been hindered by vanishing gradients during backpropagation, limiting their capacity. In response, the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) cell was developed to mitigate this issue, but it still falls behind state-of-the-art models like transformers in terms of performance. To address these limitations, we introduce the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel neural cell architecture that leverages the stability properties of Legendre Memory, a mathematical concept from differential equations. By incorporating Legendre Memory into a neural network, we can eliminate the need for a traditional LSTM cell component, such as the forget gate, thereby simplifying the architecture. Our experiments demonstrate that LMUs achieve superior performance on various tasks, including language modeling, both in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and they are more adaptable to different tasks than LSTMs. Notably, we found that LMUs can achieve comparable performance to transformers on the large-scale language modeling task using the LM, while being significantly more memory-efficient. In the first phase, a sequence of over-approximations is generated to bound the set of states reached by the program, and in the second phase, a sequence of under-approximations is generated to bound the set of states from which the program is executed. This paper presents a new approach called Adaptable Abstract Interpretation, which aims to integrate both phases into a single, adaptable sequence of abstract states. This is achieved by developing a new abstract domain called Adapta, which can represent both over- and under-approximations, and allows the representation of pre- and postconditions. The paper demonstrates the Adapta domain's ability to model a broad range of abstract interpretations, and shows that it can be used to compute both over- and under-approximations. The paper also presents a prototype implementation of the Adapta domain, and demonstrates its effectiveness on a range of benchmarks. The results show that Adapta can achieve better precision than traditional abstract interpretations, and can be used to model complex program analyses, such as dataflow analyses and abstract transformers. The sentiment analysis subfield of natural language processing contributes significantly to recommender systems, particularly in predicting user ratings. This paper introduces a novel sentiment analysis approach grounded in real-world rating prediction. Unlike existing methods, it formulates rating prediction as a sentiment regression task, leveraging the expertise of NLP and sentiment analysis. This approach employs a neural network to predict user ratings based on the sentiment they convey, using a combined model that integrates both NLP and recommender systems. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, surpassing state-of-the-art performance on MovieLens datasets. Notably, the sentiment-aware model achieves a 0.19 absolute improvement in predicted ratings compared to traditional recommender system methods. This paper presents a pioneering effort to bridge the gap between sentiment analysis and recommender systems, paving the way for future research in this area. The code and dataset used in this research are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhongdi-zhang/Sentiment-aware-Rating-Prediction. In various applications involving mesh-based computations, hexahedral elements are often the preferred choice due to their suitability for numerical computations.  However, in practical scenarios, these elements are frequently replaced by prismatic elements in many simulations.  Although prismatic elements are commonly used, there is a lack of understanding regarding why they are used instead of hexahedral elements.  In this research, a comprehensive study is conducted to investigate the impact of small distortions in hexahedral elements on the accuracy of numerical computations in two key applications: Poisson's equation and linear elasticity.  By employing a high-order finite element method, the accuracy of these computations is evaluated in terms of the $L^2$ and $H^1$ norms.  The results indicate that when hexahedral elements are slightly distorted, resulting in prismatic elements, minimal degradation in accuracy occurs, with an error rate of $O(h^2 (\ln h)^{3/2} / N_C^{1/2})$.  The computational experiments conducted support the theoretical findings, demonstrating that for a wide range of distortions, the accuracy of numerical computations remains unaffected.  The research findings suggest that for many real-world applications, using prismatic elements instead of hexahedral elements may not have a significant impact on the accuracy of numerical computations.  The research also opens up avenues for exploring the impact of more severe distortions on the accuracy of numerical computations. The objective of relation extraction is to identify relationships between entities within text data.  Conventional approaches rely on manually crafted rules, but recent advancements in machine learning have led to improved performance without the need for carefully designed features.  This study explores the potential of using transformer models, which excel in language tasks, for relation extraction.  By pre-training a model on unlabelled data and fine-tuning it on the specific task, we can leverage its built-in knowledge to effectively interpret new words and phrases.  This approach, however, assumes that the model's understanding remains consistent throughout the training process.  In reality, the model's knowledge may evolve over time due to the influence of new data, a phenomenon we investigate in this study.  Our findings indicate that the model's understanding of new entities and relationships is initially limited to general associations, but it gradually becomes more precise as it processes more data.  This study contributes to the understanding of how transformer models learn through exposure to new data and suggests that the performance of relation extraction can be enhanced by incorporating additional general knowledge. Experimental results show that agents trained with this framework perform better in scenarios with partners of different abilities and exhibit more adaptable behavior. Additionally, the generated "stupid" agent behaviors contribute to the acceleration of MARL training and provide valuable insights for debugging purposes. We've developed a set of seven quantifiable measures to evaluate the degree of complexity in the morphological development of languages. These measures are based on the principle that as a language becomes more complex, it tends to increase the variability of word lengths. We applied these metrics to data from 40 languages at various stages of development, including 28 that are considered standard examples of agglutinative languages and 12 languages from the Americas, primarily indigenous languages that have been less studied in terms of their morphological structure. We used statistical analysis to compare our new metrics with existing measures of morphological complexity, finding that the first principal component accounts for nearly 80% of the variation among the 40 languages, with our new measures significantly contributing to this understanding. Notably, our new metrics suggest that the morphological structure of indigenous languages of the Americas exhibits a unique pattern of complexity, differing from that of European languages and distinct from the patterns seen in languages undergoing or resisting grammaticalization. Our findings also indicate that the morphological structure of these indigenous languages is more similar to that of languages from the same geographic region than to languages from other parts of the world. Overall, our new metrics enhance our understanding of the morphological structure of languages and shed new light on the complex relationships between linguistic variables. We believe that our new approach can be applied to a broader range of linguistic domains, such as phonology and syntax. We have conducted a comprehensive study of galaxy substructures within the Milky Way, utilizing data from Gaia's early third data release and the Dark Matter Outrageous Fortune (DMOF) code. The DMOF code allows for the simulation of self-interacting dark matter by adjusting its interaction cross-section, which affects the density profile of substructures. Our analysis reveals that substructure density profiles are highly sensitive to the dark matter interaction cross-section. Substructures in the Milky Way exhibit a steeper density profile than predicted by standard cold dark matter simulations, which can be matched by self-interacting dark matter simulations at lower mass scales. However, at higher mass scales, the required interaction cross-section becomes unrealistically large. Our results suggest that self-interacting dark matter may not be able to explain the density profiles of substructures in the Milky Way, which could indicate the need for alternative models of dark matter interactions or a more complex baryonic influence on substructure formation. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding (RTB) allows publishers to rapidly sell available ad inventory to multiple bidders. As a result, advertisers must rapidly determine their optimal bids, taking into account the ad's value, cost per impression, the probability of conversion, and their level of risk tolerance. This study examines how different levels of risk preference and uncertainty about the ad's value affect bidding strategies. By integrating a theoretical model of optimal bidding with empirical data, we investigate how risk preferences and uncertainty interact to influence bidding decisions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the average bidder in the market is not accurately modeling their optimal bidding behavior, particularly in terms of risk tolerance. This research provides a foundation for future investigations into the bidding process. The findings also highlight the need for further exploration into how bidders adapt to uncertainty and how this impacts the market equilibrium. Ultimately, our results suggest that the ad exchange market may not always operate in a manner that maximizes revenue for advertisers. Consequently, the question of whether this suboptimal behavior can be mitigated through the use of automated bidding strategies remains an open area of inquiry. Human feedback is often required to guide reward learning, but current approaches can be impractical due to the cost and difficulty of obtaining relevant feedback. To address this issue, we propose a new framework called HATs, which enables humans to provide more efficient feedback by labeling key states in a trajectory rather than evaluating entire episodes. By focusing on critical moments, this approach can take advantage of prior knowledge and reduce the need for as many labels as would be needed to evaluate entire episodes. We test our framework in a complex real-world task, namely a robotic assembly problem, and demonstrate that it can be more effective and efficient than existing methods. Specifically, we find that HATs requires significantly fewer human labels to achieve the same performance as other methods, and that the learned policy is more robust to unexpected situations. By reducing the number of human labels required, HATs also enables more rapid exploration of the reward space and leads to a more robust policy. Overall, our results show that HATs is a useful framework for efficient human-in-the-loop reward learning. We develop a novel method for estimating the causal effect of a treatment on a variable of interest based on a complex network of interconnected variables. This approach builds on the principles of two-time point observational studies and incorporates the partial observation of key variables that influence the treatment but not the outcome. By leveraging this information, we can estimate the causal effect by which the network variables evolve over time. To achieve this, we employ a two-step process involving the integration of multiple probability models. Initially, we estimate the probability distribution of the treatment and outcome variables given the partial observations of the adjusting variables. Subsequently, we calculate the probability distribution of the treatment and outcome variables as if the adjusting variables were fully observed, while utilizing the previously estimated distribution. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our method provides accurate causal effect estimates when key variables are influenced by a common factor. The results indicate that maternal employment has a negligible impact on the cognitive abilities of children. However, we do find that maternal employment has a significant negative effect on the language abilities of children, albeit with considerable uncertainty. We introduce an unsupervised method, Self-Supervised Cross-Sectional Activity Parsing (SSCAP), for segmenting activities in videos without annotations. The approach relies on cross-sectional video pairs captured simultaneously, which often contain synchronization discrepancies. Experimental results indicate that SSCAP outperforms supervised and other unsupervised approaches in activity parsing tasks. Moreover, SSCAP's ability to infer contextual activity transitions in cross-sectional video pairs is validated through qualitative analysis of video snippets. The proposed SSCAP method offers a novel, efficient, and effective solution for segmenting activities in videos without annotations. Domain adaptation has become a crucial machine learning technique, enabling the transfer of knowledge from a source domain to a target domain despite differing distributions. A particular challenge in domain adaptation is handling labeled data scarcity in the target domain. To address this limitation, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning approach that leverages a dual framework to improve target domain performance. Firstly, we implement a semi-supervised mutual enhancement technique to refine target domain labels using unlabeled target data and pseudo-labels. Secondly, we develop a cross-domain self-supervised learning method that extracts target domain features from unlabeled data using a contrastive learning framework. Notably, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple domain adaptation benchmarks, including the Office-31 and VOC-SBD datasets. We've demonstrated a method for determining the maximum entropy that can be achieved through boson sampling, which involves calculating the probability distribution of photon counts from a multi-mode laser field. By employing a Gaussian approximation and a saddle-point analysis, we derived an equation that predicts the maximum entropy as a function of the number of modes and photon average occupancy. Notably, our result shows that the maximum entropy increases logarithmically with the number of modes, which aligns with previous findings. However, we found that this growth is accelerated by a factor related to the photon average occupancy. To validate our theoretical model, we compared its predictions to Monte Carlo simulations and found a strong agreement for a wide range of photon occupancies and mode numbers. The outcome of this study provides a useful approximation for calculating the maximum entropy in boson sampling, which can be employed in future experiments to assess the performance of photonic devices and evaluate the capabilities of boson sampling simulators based on artificial neural networks. Furthermore, our model may be applied to other boson sampling scenarios, such as those involving time-bin photonic boxes, which are being explored in recent research. We introduce Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), a novel approach that projects temporal sequences into a lower-dimensional, time-aware space while considering the relationships between points in sequence. By utilizing a unique tensor representation, our model leverages the benefits of Isomap and Siamese networks to create a space that preserves temporal relationships and identifies patterns common across sequences. The algorithm's key strength lies in its ability to pinpoint critical sequence points, or "diffing" points, which significantly enhance model interpretability. Empirical evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate SGTM-TT's superiority over established methods in both accuracy and interpretability. Notably, our model's performance surpasses state-of-the-art results in Visual Question Answering (VQA) without relying on object detection or attention mechanisms. These outcomes provide valuable insights for the practical implementation of reinforcement learning algorithms using recurrent neural networks.  Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to the development of efficient reinforcement learning methods that can effectively tackle complex problems. This study introduces a novel image copy detection task, where the goal is to identify transformed copies of a query image, involving common operations like cropping, resizing, and format changes. We examine the vulnerability of current detectors to these image transformations and investigate how they impact performance. We also present a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 1 million images, derived from 1000 images, to assess the robustness of detectors in various scenarios. The results reveal that different transformations have varying levels of difficulty, with cropping being the most challenging. Furthermore, we observe that resizing and format changes often facilitate cropping, while cropping can occur independently or in combination with other transformations. We also find that state-of-the-art detectors struggle with transformed images, particularly those with high levels of cropping. To address these limitations, we propose a straightforward yet effective method, called Cropped Region Embedding (CRE), to improve copy detection. CRE involves embedding cropped regions of the query image into a detector's database, leading to a notable increase in detection rates for transformed copies. We validate the effectiveness of CRE through extensive experiments on our benchmark dataset and demonstrate its potential for real-world applications. The code and dataset are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyizhang/CopyDetectionTransformed. Additionally, we invite researchers to participate in a challenge to further enhance the performance of copy detectors on transformed images. The challenge can be accessed at https://www.challengedata.withgoogle.com/challenge/CopyDetectionTransformed. We believe that CRE provides a solid foundation for future research and development in this area. Ultimately, we hope that our work will inspire the creation of more robust and versatile image copy detection methods that can effectively handle transformed copies. These methods will have significant implications for real-world applications in image search, content management, and digital forensics. The performance of the proposed CRE method is comparable to the state-of-the-art detector, FPT, and outperforms other detectors on transformed images. The results show that CRE achieves a recall of 0.8131 at a precision of 0.9999, while FPT reaches a recall of 0.7631 at the same precision. Approximate query operations, specifically membership checking, have garnered significant attention in recent years, with applications extending to networked systems and distributed storage. Researchers have proposed various probabilistic techniques to achieve this goal, with some methods utilizing filters to speed up query processing. However, existing filters have limitations, particularly high false positive rates, which can be costly in certain contexts. To address this issue, we introduce two new families of filters designed to minimize false positives: the first, based on the concept of $\ell_1$-norm distance, and the second, incorporating a level of redundancy. We evaluate the trade-offs between these filters' size, speed, and accuracy, as well as their performance under both static and dynamic data sets. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of combining multiple filters to achieve optimal results. Our comprehensive analysis provides valuable insights for practitioners to select the most suitable filter for their specific use case. Ultimately, we present a dynamic data structure that leverages these new filters to achieve low false positive rates, with experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness. The proposed filter and data structure are available for public use. The associated code can be found at the URL provided in the author information.

High-resolution simulations of DNA and RNA require accurate modeling of bond angles and bond lengths. We have developed a new DNA/RNA model that allows for precise control over these parameters in all-atom simulations. Our new model is based on the widely used CHARMM force field and includes six key rotational degrees of freedom that can be customized to match experimental data. We validated our model by simulating short double-stranded DNA sequences using both constant length and constant length simulations. Our results show that the model effectively maintains a constant helical repeat and sugar pucker phase, while also exhibiting expected variations in torsion angles and base pair orientations. Additionally, our model accurately reproduces the behavior of specific DNA sequences at high temperatures, while constant length simulations reveal subtle differences in melting behavior. Our new model provides a powerful tool for studying DNA and RNA structures, allowing for precise adjustments to key parameters and insights into their dynamic behavior. We anticipate that this model will be useful for investigating the structural and dynamic properties of DNA and RNA at high resolution. This research presents a comprehensive analysis of recent advancements in swarm drones for military applications, focusing on those published between 2018 and 2021. Due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic in 2019 and 2020, our assessment is based on a smaller time frame than initially intended, nonetheless providing a thorough overview of the rapidly evolving field. A total of 222 relevant studies were selected from the databases Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, with the majority (63.6%) published in 2019 and 2020. Our analysis includes a detailed examination of 222 studies, with a special emphasis on 40 notable cases that have significantly impacted the field. Furthermore, we have categorized the remaining studies according to five key aspects: problem formulation, system design, implementation, simulation, and evaluation. This research aims to offer a valuable insight into the current state of the art, identify knowledge gaps, and inform future research directions in the field of military swarm drones. In the study of contagious diseases, researchers have traditionally focused on modeling the spread of infections within a static, fixed population.  However, real-world scenarios often involve tracking the progression of an outbreak among a dynamic group of individuals.  To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that clusters individuals based on their shared infection history and state trajectory.  By grouping similar subjects, our method enables researchers to analyze the spread of diseases in an out-of-order population, offering insights into both the evolution of an epidemic and the characteristics of its constituent clusters.  Through simulations and analysis of a SIR model, we demonstrate that our approach successfully identifies cohesive groups of individuals, accurately estimates their number, and accurately reconstructs the evolution of the epidemic.  Furthermore, we apply our method to a real-world COVID-19 contact tracing dataset, uncovering intriguing patterns in the behavior of individuals within these groups.  Notably, our results suggest that certain subjects engage in prolonged interactions with the same cluster, potentially increasing the transmission risk.  Overall, our method provides a powerful framework for understanding contagious disease spread within a dynamic, out-of-order population. We introduce a novel method for generating a likelihood function in the context of CMB map-making, which allows us to directly optimize a set of parameters related to instrumental and data acquisition flaws. This approach is based on a simplified statistical model, which assumes that data errors can be attributed to a combination of noise, instrumental imperfections, data gaps, and systematic errors. By leveraging this simplified model, we develop a maximum likelihood estimator that maximizes the likelihood function with respect to the parameters in question. However, this estimator is susceptible to inaccuracies stemming from incomplete data acquisition, instrumental imperfections, and other sources of model errors. To mitigate these inaccuracies, we propose an iterative method for refining the parameters, which relies on an initial CMB map. This method is subsequently applied to a selection of real and simulated CMB maps, yielding parameter estimates that closely align with their true values. Notably, our method demonstrates its effectiveness across a range of data sets, including those from the Planck satellite and simulated data at the level of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of model errors and identify potential avenues for further research aimed at addressing these inaccuracies. In a learning framework, this issue can lead to incorrect knowledge acquisition by the learner. In this research, we investigate how the teacher can modify their communication to minimize ambiguity and ensure the learner accurately understands their intent. We establish a model where the teacher and learner have access to object features, allowing them to assess the likelihood of ambiguity before communication. The teacher then responds with a message that maximizes the learner's understanding while minimizing ambiguity. We demonstrate that the optimal teacher message is based on a specific query and provide a bounded approximation for the optimal message. Experimental results indicate that the teacher's modified communication significantly reduces errors and achieves near-optimal performance. Furthermore, we explore an extension where the teacher is aware of the learner's prior knowledge and demonstrate that the teacher's communication strategy remains unaffected. In contrast, we show that if the teacher is not informed about the learner's prior knowledge, the optimal learning strategy involves the teacher inquiring about the specific object of interest. We validate these findings through numerical experiments. Overall, this research highlights the importance of referential ambiguity in communication and provides a foundation for further investigation into the relationship between ambiguity and communication. The research also showcases the potential for the teacher to adapt their communication strategy to account for the learner's prior knowledge, leading to improved understanding and reduced errors. In this research, we address the issue of identifying direct and indirect effects under a stratified case-control design, where the primary goal is to evaluate how a binary exposure, A, influences an outcome, Y, through a binary intermediate variable, M. Stratified designs are particularly useful in examining the effects of exposures on disease risks in specific subgroups, such as age groups. However, conventional methods for estimating direct and indirect effects are not applicable in stratified designs, as they rely on the assumption of equal probabilities of selection, which is not met in case-control designs. We propose a new approach that takes into account the design's characteristics and provides asymptotic validity. We also demonstrate the method's performance through simulation experiments and apply it to a real-world example examining the effect of body mass index on cardiovascular disease risk through left ventricular mass in the Framingham Heart Study. The results show that our method accurately estimates direct and indirect effects in stratified designs and highlights the significant pathways through hypertension and left ventricular wall thickness from body mass index to cardiovascular disease risk. These results have important implications for developing targeted interventions to prevent cardiovascular disease in specific populations. Notably, our method outperforms existing approaches on multiple medical imaging tasks, including detecting rare diseases and understanding the structure of organs. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves optimal regret for non-stochastic, delay-prone bandits and experts. This model encompasses scenarios with non-stochastic rewards, delayed arrivals (up to $d$ time units), and adversarially chosen actions (up to $K$ options). Our algorithm ensures an upper bound on regret that scales polynomially with $d$, with a specific exponent related to the trade-off between delayed arrivals and expert actions. When $d$ is large, it yields a regret that grows slowly with time, while a large number of expert actions ($K$) yields a regret that grows slowly with the number of expert actions. This trade-off is not present in existing settings. We demonstrate that our algorithm's regret performance closely matches the established lower bounds for both bandits and experts, with the added consideration of delayed arrivals. This work significantly expands on previous research, offering a novel framework that bridges delayed bandits and experts with additional structure. We also provide a detailed analysis of our algorithm's design, highlighting its key components and how they contribute to the trade-off. Our results are validated through numerical experiments that show our algorithm's performance closely matches theoretical predictions. This work opens new avenues for exploring delayed learning problems, with the potential to extend our findings to other areas. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential for reinforcement learning to significantly impact the diversity of words used in dialogue interactions. Furthermore, an analysis of the generated responses reveals that the model's diversity predictions are highly accurate, and the model is capable of generating more diverse responses over time. Overall, our model provides a practical solution for improving the diversity of task-oriented dialogue systems. The code and pre-trained models are available online.

We investigate symplectic geometry on complex projective spaces $CP(V)$ of weights $(1,\dots,1)$ with $|V|>1$, focusing on those with a symplectic connection. It's observed that these spaces have a distinct characteristic: they can't support a compatible flat connection. This leads to the exploration of their curvature properties when the symplectic connection is chosen adaptively. Furthermore, we establish that among all symplectic projective spaces of weights $(1,\dots,1)$ with $|V|\geq 2$, those studied here possess the most negative curvature. This result extends a previous finding by R. Bryant for the case where $|V|=2$. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings in the context of the Calabi conjecture. Finally, we outline a potential approach to constructing a complete noncompact symplectic projective space of weight $(1,\dots,1)$ with a negative curvature, using the Kähler-Einstein metric on the Grassmannian $Gr(2,4)$ as a model. This method could potentially yield a complete noncompact symplectic projective space of weight $(1,\dots,1)$ with a negative curvature, although it remains uncertain whether such a construction is feasible. The curvature of the loss surface in deep learning models determines the effectiveness of training methods, particularly when using first or second-order optimization algorithms. Despite the importance of the Hessian or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation, direct computation is impractical due to memory constraints and time complexity. We present a novel method to approximate the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix without computing the full Hessian, leveraging the sparsity of the Hessian matrix and an efficient sampling strategy to reduce memory usage and computational time. Our approach is evaluated on various ResNet models and demonstrates significant time savings while achieving comparable convergence rates with and without access to the full Hessian. We also explore the practical implications of using an approximate Hessian for hyperparameter tuning. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alegrosotto/hessian_approximation.

inanimate objects in languages that assign gender to such entities. We discovered 
that in languages with gendered inanimate nouns, words of the same gender tend 
to cluster together in the same spatial area within the word embedding space. 
This phenomenon suggests that inanimate object representations are shaped, at 
least in part, by their grammatical gender. We further found that this effect is 
more pronounced in languages with a stronger distinction between inanimate noun 
gender categories. This finding implies that word embeddings can reveal 
grammatically-driven associations for inanimate objects, which could have 
implications for areas like robotics and law. We also developed a method to 
detect whether a word has been assigned a gender in a specific language. This 
method can be used to identify words that have been gendered in languages that 
do not typically assign gender to inanimate nouns. We found that English, a 
language where inanimate nouns are typically gendered, exhibits a significant 
number of such words. These words are often represented in word embeddings as 
being more similar to their animate counterparts. This suggests that English 
embeddings retain a remnant of the grammatical distinction seen in other 
languages. We also found that this distinction can be exploited to improve the 
performance of English language models in tasks like sentiment analysis. The

Our approach, called ZeroShotPose, enables pose estimation for novel objects without training models for each object category. It relies on a pre-trained model that can predict object categories and perform pose estimation tasks in a task-agnostic manner. Given an image, our method uses the object category predicted by the pre-trained model to simulate the predicted pose. We demonstrate that fine-tuning the pre-trained model's pose component significantly improves performance. Additionally, we found that integrating a category-conditioned model, which takes the object category into account, enhances our results. Through comprehensive experiments on LineMOD, LineMOD-6, LineMOD-17, and T-LESS datasets, we found that ZeroShotPose achieves better performance than models specifically trained for object categories in the LineMOD-6 dataset. Notably, our method outpermits the state-of-the-art model, DPOSE, on the T-LESS dataset by 4.5% mean average precision. Our findings suggest that ZeroShotPose provides a versatile solution for pose estimation on novel objects without extensive model retraining. vector-based and structure-based approaches. The vector-based approach 
utilizes pre-trained embeddings that can be projected onto a common space 
for zero-shot cross-lingual retrieval. Conversely, structure-based methods 
involve translating a query into its source equivalent using machine 
translation and then employing monolingual retrieval. This research seeks to 
bridge the gap between these two methods by introducing a new framework that 
combines the strengths of both. The proposed framework, called Cross-lingual 
Reranking, aims to enhance the retrieval results of both vector-based and 
structure-based approaches through a single reranking stage. This is 
accomplished by merging the top results from both methods and subjecting them 
to a joint ranking process. The results of our experiments demonstrate that 
Cross-lingual Reranking successfully elevates the performance of both vector- 
and structure-based approaches, ultimately achieving state-of-the-art results on 
cross-lingual retrieval. The code for our proposed method is publicly

A novel neural architecture search approach, called Differentiation of Parallel Children, is introduced in this paper. DPC, a method inspired by the process of differentiation in biology, allows multiple child models to share resources while exploring vast model configurations. During training, the gradients of a shared operator with respect to the objective loss are computed across all child models, resulting in the accumulation of gradients. This process, referred to as "interference," increases the impact of gradients on the shared operator, effectively prioritizing its parameters. As the number of shared operators is reduced, the accumulation of gradients leads to significant parameter updates, while multiple unique operators result in minimal accumulation, resulting in minimal updates. This innovative technique enables the efficient exploration of large neural architecture spaces, particularly in resource-constrained settings. We investigated the resilience of neural network substructures when faced with significant data perturbations, random input modifications, and non-adversarial noise. To this end, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the robustness properties of various neural network architectures and their subcomponents. Notably, we found that the remaining connections within the pruned networks, which are primarily between nearby layers, exhibit a pronounced spatial pattern, suggesting a potential optimization opportunity. Building upon this insight, we developed a novel pruning strategy, dubbed'spatial pruning', which aims to minimize spatial connections. This approach outperformed traditional pruning methods by reducing computational costs, while achieving comparable or even improved performance. Specifically, we observed a significant reduction in computational complexity, with the pruned ResNet50 model achieving a 34.7% decrease in FLOPs, while maintaining or even improving accuracy. This research offers valuable insights for designing more efficient and robust neural networks. The code and pruned models are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengxizhang/spatial-pruning. Additionally, we released a robustness benchmark at https://github.com/zhengxizhang/robust-benchmark, which allows for the evaluation of neural network robustness against various types of perturbations. This benchmark is intended to facilitate further research in this area. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of considering the spatial structure of neural networks in order to enhance their robustness and efficiency. A significant challenge in legged locomotion is navigating complex, yielding ground conditions. To address this issue, researchers have developed novel force control methods for legged robots. However, existing approaches often rely on simplified models of ground characteristics, neglecting the complexities involved. In this study, we present a pioneering force control method grounded in the principles of variational inequality constraints. This method takes into account the ground's nonlinear properties, represented by a polyhedral convex set, and utilizes a projected gradient descent strategy to optimize control inputs. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted a series of experiments on a rigid terrain and a deformable ground surface, demonstrating the controller's ability to adapt to changing ground conditions. Notably, our controller successfully replicated the desired ground reaction forces on both surfaces, and demonstrated improved performance in walking trials. The results indicate that our approach can efficiently and accurately regulate the ground reaction forces of legged robots in various ground conditions. The primary goal is to identify and visualize deviations between the expected model behavior and observed traces. This research introduces a new method, the Conformity Cloud, to visualize and measure conformity for entire process model families in relation to multiple, trace-based benchmarks. The proposed technique visualizes and measures conformity for any process model family and associated trace-based benchmark, offering a more comprehensive understanding of system performance. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the Conformance Cloud through a simulation experiment and showcases its practical application using real-life data from two different domains. The results show that the Conformance Cloud facilitates the identification of process model families that accurately simulate real processes and accurately predict process performance. Additionally, the results reveal that the Conformance Cloud enables the detection of poorly performing process model configurations. The study concludes that the Conformance Cloud offers a versatile and effective technique for analyzing process performance in different domains. A novel semantics framework for temporal planning has been developed, providing
a flexible and comprehensive approach to capture diverse interpretation of
temporal constraints. This generic semantics can be instantiated to specific
interpreations, enabling comparison and evaluation of existing as well as proposed
time-based planning models. Furthermore, we introduce a universal time unit
model, a specific instance of our semantics, which can serve as a benchmark for
assessing the performance of planners in handling temporal constraints. An
experimental evaluation is conducted to examine how different time unit
representations influence solution times in various planning benchmarks. Our
results demonstrate that using an abstract time unit representation can result in
substantial time savings for many planning benchmarks, often by several orders of
magnitude. This study underscores the importance of carefully considering the time
representation in temporal planning. All implementation details are made publicly
available through the planning toolkit, LPGplan. An accompanying technical report
provides a more in-depth exploration of our semantics and experimental analysis.

The integration of camera and LiDAR sensors in autonomous driving systems has led to a prominent 3D object detection method, known as fusion. However, this approach is not suitable when one component fails due to sensor malfunctions, adverse weather conditions, or collisions. In this research, we introduce a novel camera-based 3D object detection method that operates independently, without relying on LiDAR data. This approach leverages a deep learning framework to process raw camera data and generate 3D object proposals. To enhance its effectiveness, we develop a method to simulate LiDAR beam rays and calculate corresponding 2D projections, which enables our method to utilize fusion-based training data. Experimental results on the Waymo Open Dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms existing fusion-based detectors when one sensor is disabled, and achieves comparable performance under normal conditions. Notably, our method surpasses all previous fusion-based detectors in terms of detection accuracy when both sensors are functioning. Additionally, we propose a new fusion strategy to integrate our method with a fusion-based detector, which achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Waymo Open Dataset. Artificial neural networks' impressive object recognition capabilities on established benchmarks have left many wondering if they truly understand visual information or simply excel due to statistical correlations. To investigate this further, we conducted a study where we tested ANNs' and humans' abilities to recognize objects under various difficult image conditions, including extreme brightness, color distortion, and pixelation. Our results show ANNs consistently fail to match human performance across all scenarios, suggesting ANNs' successes might be due to relying on simplistic visual cues rather than true visual understanding. This raises questions about the reliability of ANNs' performance in real-world applications and highlights the need for further improvements in these models. To facilitate future research, we are releasing our experimental setup and data on ANNs' performance so others can replicate our findings and develop more effective models. Our study also provides valuable insights for researchers working on machine learning and computer vision, encouraging the exploration of new methods that can better mimic human visual perception and learning processes. By shedding light on the limitations of ANNs, our research aims to pave the way for future breakthroughs in these models and their applications. Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of continued efforts to bridge the gap between human and machine learning, ultimately achieving true artificial intelligence. To investigate the possibility of electroweak baryogenesis through a Sphaleron process, we examine a model with an extended scalar sector that exhibits a first-order phase transition and meets the conditions for successful reheating via oscillations of the Higgs field. We analyze the scalar potential in two distinct scenarios and identify the necessary conditions for these scenarios to be physically valid. We then calculate the energy released during the phase transition and the resulting entropy produced, taking into account the impact of radiation and the scalar field on the system. We also determine the required initial energy for the Sphaleron process and the corresponding baryon asymmetry generated, given that the universe undergoes a Sphaleron process at the phase transition temperature. This study introduces an advanced diagnostic framework for identifying COVID-19 from lung CT images using cutting-edge technology based on the Double Attention-guided Transformer (DAT) architecture. The framework incorporates two key components: a Double Attention module that enhances feature extraction and selection, and a multi-head attention mechanism. The proposed approach was evaluated using two COVID-19 datasets, with COVID19-CT-Dataset yielding a high accuracy rate of 96.67% and the RSNA-Pneumonia Dataset achieving a high Area Under the Curve score of 0.97. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to support clinicians in making informed diagnoses and to aid in the development of more effective COVID-19 treatments. A new sensitivity analysis method is developed to address concerns about biased conclusions due to missing outcome data, which cannot be recovered even with extensive data collection. This approach involves using causal inference models to create counterfactual outcomes for individuals with missing data, drawing on observed data from similar subjects within the same study. A simulation-based evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in handling various types of missing data, including both random and systematic patterns. The proposed technique is then applied to a real-world study examining the effects of a treatment on blood pressure, with results highlighting the potential for biased findings if not properly accounted for missing data. This method is presented as a practical tool for researchers to identify and mitigate biases stemming from missing outcome data. Further research could involve expanding this method to accommodate multiple types of missing data, incorporating external information, and applying it to diverse fields of study. As smart cities expand, they generate an increasing amount of data, which is used to develop intelligent systems that improve urban life. However, this data is often limited by its reliance on current sensor technology. To address this limitation, we present CitySpec, a framework for specifying and predicting the appearance of future smart city sensors. This involves analyzing existing sensor data and generating synthetic images of the city, both now and in its future state. This framework enables us to create high-quality training datasets for current sensors and simulate how the city will look with new, upcoming sensors. By combining real and synthetic data, we train a more robust model that can accurately predict the city's appearance over time. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that our model performs significantly better on both existing and future sensor scenarios. This framework provides a valuable tool for researchers and developers to anticipate and prepare for the impact of future sensor technologies. Our code and data are available for public use. state-of-the-art results without fine-tuning, but they often struggle with
generalizing to new tasks due to their rigid fine-grained representations.

transforming CLIP's image-text embeddings into a unified semantic space.
Our method, called SEED, uses a self-supervised objective to preserve the
distances between these embeddings, allowing for more flexible and robust
representation learning. Experimental results demonstrate that SEED leads to
substantial improvements in CLIP's performance on a range of tasks, while
also enhancing its transferability and robustness under various data
perturbations. Notably, SEED achieves state-of-the-art results on open-book
question answering and zero-shot object detection without requiring additional
training. Our code and models are publicly available on GitHub.

to a significant amount of radiation, which has led researchers to explore lower-dose and
ultra-low-dose CT scans as an alternative. These scans provide comparable image quality
while minimizing radiation exposure. Building on this idea, we propose a new deep
learning method to detect COVID-19 using low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans. Our
approach involves training a model using the ResNet-50 architecture and fine-tuning it
with the ResNet-101 pre-trained network. We tested our method on the official COVID19
dataset, which includes 5,000 positive cases and 5,000 negative cases. Our results show

AUC of 0.977 and a loss of 0.044. Additionally, we found that our method can handle
ultra-low-dose CT scans with an AUC of 0.971 and a loss of 0.051. Our method's

exposure by 90% and 99%, respectively. Overall, our method provides a reliable and

As a dictionary, it offers several benefits: (1) it streamlines browsing by automatically suggesting potential vocabulary based on sentence previews, (2) it provides detailed statistics on selected vocabulary, and (3) it offers a comprehensive vocabulary list for easy study. Through experiments, we demonstrate DictGen's effectiveness in vocabulary learning and its ability to outperform human competitors in a word-filling task. Additionally, we showcase DictGen's capabilities in sentence generation and word prediction. Finally, we present DictGen's performance in sentence generation and word prediction on various datasets. This study examines the connection between COVID-19 news coverage and the spread of the virus in the US using a novel approach that combines large datasets and a sophisticated model to track topic-based trends over time. Our analysis reveals distinct patterns in local and national news narratives, with a shift from initial focus on travel restrictions to widespread hospitalization and death coverage. Notably, our findings indicate that local news coverage initially aligned more closely with national death rates than state-specific case counts, but over time this alignment shifted towards a stronger correlation with state-specific case counts. This research highlights the importance of using news coverage as an early indicator of the pandemic's progression and the need for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between local and national trends. Additionally, our analysis of the Biden Administration's COVID-19 news coverage suggests that the shift in national discourse may have contributed to increased awareness and compliance with mitigation efforts. Overall, our approach provides a framework for exploring the complex interplay between news narratives and the spread of the pandemic. As such, this research has significant implications for public health policymakers and practitioners seeking to leverage news as a tool for early detection, risk assessment, and targeted interventions. Efficient data usage is crucial for both imitation and reinforcement learning, particularly when real data is scarce and expensive to obtain. We introduce a novel approach that generates synthetic experiences in addition to utilizing real data. The generated experiences are tailored to mimic policies that are likely to produce valuable information. We then combine the synthetic and real data using a novel weighting strategy that prioritizes the real data's ability to improve performance. Through this approach, we achieve better results than traditional methods that only rely on real data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method across various tasks, including those with high-dimensional observations and large action spaces. We successfully apply our method to learn from real data in robotic manipulation and game environments, such as Atari games. Our code is available for public access.

Furthermore, we propose a new learning strategy that balances the benefits of probability-matching and all-or-nothing approaches, and we verify its effectiveness through simulations. We anticipate that our research will contribute to a deeper understanding of stochastic learning and may inspire new insights into the decision-making processes of both artificial and biological agents. By incorporating cause-effect explanations, we aim to enhance human understanding of the robot's control principles and foster trust in assistive teleoperation applications. The results demonstrate that our explanations successfully clarified the robot's behavior, leading to a significant increase in human trust. Additionally, we found that the robot's performance improved when users were provided with these explanations, as they were more likely to delegate control to the robot. Overall, our research indicates that the clarity of robot explanations has a substantial impact on assistive teleoperation interactions. This effect can be studied using the mean-field Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) model, which describes how the electrostatic potential around the surface changes due to the solvent's dielectric properties and ion behavior. However, the PB model's predictions are often at odds with experimental findings, leading researchers to consider more complex models, such as the PB model with ion size effects. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how the PB model's assumptions affect the behavior of an electrolyte solution near a charged surface. Our results show that the PB model accurately captures the solvent's dielectric effect when the ion size is negligible, but fails to do so when ion size effects are significant. Furthermore, we found that the PB model overestimates the electrostatic potential near charged surfaces due to the neglect of ion size effects, resulting in a more negative potential than what is observed in molecular dynamics simulations. This discrepancy is particularly pronounced for monovalent ions, which have a small size, and is less pronounced for multivalent ions. This study highlights the importance of considering ion size effects when modeling electrolyte solutions using the PB model, especially for systems involving monovalent ions. Furthermore, the review covers the challenges associated with experimental realization and the necessity for more in-depth theoretical investigations in this area. Ultimately, the review concludes with an exploration of the potential for future research and the significant hurdles that need to be overcome to achieve practical applications based on YSR states. As such, the review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge and the promising avenues for future research in this field.

in conjunction with knowledge distillation on reducing the computational burden
of large language models. We examine how incorporating knowledge distillation
in combination with P-E T methods impacts the performance and efficiency of

distillation can enhance the performance of small models without increasing
the computational cost. Notably, we discovered that distillation can counteract
the performance decline observed in small models when using P-E T alone in
combination with the BERT pre-trained language model. Moreover, we found that
distillation can improve the stability of the optimization process, as evidenced
by the convergence rates of the small models. These results indicate that
incorporating knowledge distillation can be a valuable strategy for achieving
parameter efficiency in deep learning models. Our code is publicly available

We introduce a novel metric learning approach, called Pairwise Added Comparison Network, or PACE-Net. Unlike conventional metric learning methods that focus on maintaining similar distances between comparisons before and after data transformations, PACE-Net learns a more general and practical rule for comparing sets after elements are added or removed. To train this network, we employ a supervised learning strategy, where we present the comparison network with two sets as is, with an added element, and with an element removed, and ask it to predict the probability that the sets are essentially the same in all three cases. Experimental results demonstrate that PACE-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various real-world datasets, and can effectively handle set operations with a large number of elements. To mitigate this issue, we propose a new model that dynamically controls the attention based on the words already output, allowing it to focus more on the late generated words and ignore unnecessary early words. We introduce a new network model that blends elements from two existing models: one that accounts for preferential attachment and another that accounts for uniform attachment. Our model's degree distribution can be expressed using a single equation that incorporates a unique "bending point" separating two distinct behaviors, accurately capturing the complex patterns observed in real networks. By analyzing this distribution, we demonstrate that our model's parameters can be precisely identified, leading to a method for estimating the probability distribution of degrees in these networks. Through simulations, we validate the effectiveness of this method and apply it to study the Twitter network. The results reveal a degree distribution with a "bending point" around degree 50, indicating a transition from preferential attachment to uniform attachment. Furthermore, we observe that preferential attachment dominates in the network core, comprising influential users, while uniform attachment dominates in the periphery. This finding aligns with prior research. Additionally, we identify a group of users with moderate influence, exhibiting characteristics of a "bimodal" power law distribution. The proposed method offers a valuable tool for network analysis, enabling the identification of these two distinct behaviors and the extraction of meaningful structural insights. Our analysis also sheds light on the social implications of these findings, including the role of preferential attachment in spreading information and the impact of uniform attachment on social dynamics. Overall, our results provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex social networks underlying information dissemination. As an example of the practical application of our method, we demonstrate how it can be used to identify influential users in Twitter by analyzing the degree of a subset of users and comparing it to their actual influence as measured by retweets. The method accurately captures the characteristics of influential users, even when applied to a subset of the network. This suggests that our model can be used to build a predictive framework for identifying influential users, even when working with incomplete network data. Network analysis heavily relies on dynamic graph embedding, which underpins various applications like link prediction and node ranking. The evolution of a dynamic network can be represented as a sequence of static graphs, where each graph's structure is described by an adjacency matrix. We propose a new framework for this purpose, which involves representing each graph by a distribution over its possible future evolutions, a concept we call 'the future is now'. We then develop a method to model these distributions as a distribution over word embeddings, utilizing a variant of the Word2Vec algorithm. The resulting model, called Dyn2Vec, effectively captures the dynamic nature of networks and outperforms existing methods in predicting future graph evolutions. A tunneling spectroscopy setup has been used to analyze Fe$_7$O$_9$ thin films, 
which some researchers claim exhibit Majorana fermions at their surface. 
However, our investigation into the tunneling characteristics of Fe$_7$O$_9$ 
thin films reveals that the tunneling conductance displays a peak that 
persistently appears at low temperatures, contradicting the expected behavior 
of Majorana fermions, whose peak should diminish as the temperature drops. 
Furthermore, the observed tunneling characteristics can be explained by the 
presence of a single Kondo impurity, rather than any exotic phenomenon. 
Our findings indicate that the tunneling signal attributed to Majorana fermions 
is actually a result of the standard Kondo effect. 
The Kondo effect's influence can be eliminated by introducing a magnetic field, 
which significantly reduces the tunneling conductance's peak. 
This outcome suggests that the Kondo effect should be taken into account when 
interpreting tunneling spectroscopy data in the study of topological phases. 
Ultimately, our research underscores the necessity of distinguishing between 
exotic tunneling phenomena and more conventional ones, such as the Kondo effect.

The proposed method leverages a pre-trained CycleGAN model to map raw audio to pre-processed features, and a pre-trained ASR model to map these features to predicted transcriptions. By combining these mappings with a pre-trained transcription-to-feature model, the inter-domain loss is calculated and used to refine the CycleGAN mapping, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, the model's ability to predict transcriptions is updated using the refined features, leading to overall better results. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech and VGGSound datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving speech recognition capabilities without requiring additional labeled data. Notably, the model achieves significant relative improvements of up to 4.4% and 5.4% in character error rate on the Librispeech test-clean and test-other subsets, respectively. Active inference posits that agents actively perceive their surroundings by formulating prior beliefs and taking actions aimed at gathering more information to refine those beliefs. This process is rooted in variational Bayesian inference, with observed data serving as novel evidence that updates the agent's understanding. While successful in modeling animal behavior, the method's application to robotic systems is hindered by the difficulty of balancing exploration and exploitation. To address this challenge, we propose a novel variational message passing approach that enables active inference on robotic systems, even in scenarios with uncertain dynamics and sensor data. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments on a mobile robot navigating an environment with varying sizes and obstacles. Compared to existing methods, our approach achieves improved performance, as measured by the accuracy of the inferred environment and the reduction in collision risk. The accompanying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/utd-frcb/active_inference_for_robotics. Furthermore, a comprehensive tutorial outlining the necessary steps for active inference on robotic systems can be found on https://github.com/utd-frcb/active_inference_for_robotics/blob/main/active_inference_tutorial.ipynb. Future research directions, including the extension to multi-agent systems, are also outlined. Ultimately, our work showcases the potential of active inference to develop more sophisticated robotic systems capable of efficiently exploring and navigating complex environments.
